newsitem.title: USA: Wells Fargo shares fall on earnings warning.
newsitem.headline: Wells Fargo shares fall on earnings warning.

text.p: Wells Fargo & Co.'s stock tumbled sharply Wednesday after the bank said problems with the integration of First Interstate Bancorp would result in weaker than expected second-quarter profits.

The news, issued before the stock market opened, confirmed what many on Wall Street had already suspected: that the $11 billion merger of Wells Fargo and First Interstate, completed in April 1996, has been far from smooth.

"I got the sense that earnings would be below expectations due to revenue shortfall and customer erosion. But I thought that these non-recurring charges were behind them," said Ray Soifer, analyst with Brown Brothers Harriman. "This is bad news."
Analysts estimate the one-time expenses relating to various integration issues will range from $120 million to $140 million.

Stock in San Francisco-based Wells Fargo tumbled $18.375 to $260.625 on the New York Stock Exchange on fears the bank's problems may extend beyond the second quarter, particularly with respect to lost revenues.

"Adverse effects on Wells Fargo (from the merger) include lost revenues from fleeing customers and likely disappointing earnings, at least for the remainder of 1997," said George Salem, analyst with Gerard Klauer Mattison & Co. Inc.
On Wednesay, Wells Fargo said earnings will be about 30 percent below first-quarter 1997 earnings or about $1 per share below analysts' consensus forecast of $3.53 per share.
In the second quarter of 1996, Wells Fargo, the nation's eighth-largest bank, earned $363 million, or $3.61 a share.
Several analysts had already braced themselves for another quarter of sluggish revenues as Wells Fargo customers, angry over service disruptions, fled to other banks.

But many were caught off guard by Wells' statement Wednesday that the earnings shortfall would be due to one-time, unexpected expenses for resolution of various operational and back-office issues related to integration, including clearing accounts with other banks.

"The hole's a little deeper than we thought and we don't know how long it will take to dig themselves out of the hole," said analyst Soifer, who slashed his full-year 1997 estimate to $13.80 per share from $14.50 per share.
For 1996, Wells Fargo reported earnings of $12.21 a share.
Soifer said his 1997 estimate remained under review pending more details from Wells Fargo when it releases second-quarter earnings July 15.

Analysts said the intense battle between Wells Fargo and rival suitor First Bank System Inc. for control of First Interstate forced Wells to make dramatic cost cuts, which in turn hurt its ability to manage the much larger combination.
"To make the numbers work, they had to cut deep and fast into the cost structure of First Interstate," said analyst Thomas Theurkauf, with Keefe, Bruyette & Woods Inc.

" ... We have been in the camp that there's not a quick fix at the bank," Theurkauf said. "I hope I'm wrong but I think that when you run into problems of this sort your competitors can feed off of that literally for months and months, so I don't think they're out of the woods yet."
News of the bank's second-quarter problems is the latest in a series of bad news to hit Wells Fargo recently.
In May, billionaire investor Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway Inc. sold more than 300,000 shares of Wells Fargo, reducing his stake in the bank to around 7.8 percent.
Buffett could not be reached for comment Wednesday.
Word of the sale was followed the next day by news that President William Zuendt, one of the architects of the First Interstate acquisition, planned to retire later this year.

"Several acquaintences of Zuendt told me that he burned out on the job. There were many operational problems as a result of this merger. Some of the expenses announced today relate to these issues apparently," said one analyst.
